questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "The queue at the park gate stretched like a tired snake."
questions.explanation: The comparison between the queue and a snake is announced with *like*, which is the test for a simile. A metaphor would have said the queue *was* a tired snake. Metonymy and apostrophe are different figures entirely.

distractorRationale.a: A metaphor does not use like or as
distractorRationale.c: Nothing here stands in for an associated institution
distractorRationale.d: Nobody absent or abstract is being addressed

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "The Lagos sun was a landlord on every roof."
questions.explanation: The sun is identified with a landlord without *like* or *as*. That direct identity is a metaphor. The same picture with *like* would have been a simile. No one is being addressed, and the line is not saying the opposite of what it means.

distractorRationale.a: There is no like or as, so it is not a simile
distractorRationale.c: The sun is described, not spoken to
distractorRationale.d: Irony belongs to figures of contrast, and this line means what it pictures

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "The Harmattan coughed through the classroom windows."
questions.explanation: Coughing is a human action given to the dry wind. That is personification. There is no *like*, no associated institution standing in, and the wind is not being addressed — it is being described as if it were a person.

distractorRationale.a: No like or as appears
distractorRationale.b: The Harmattan is not standing in for something else; it is itself acting
distractorRationale.d: Apostrophe would be 'O Harmattan, leave our windows'

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Comprehension and Literature

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "O Justice, when will you visit our street?"
questions.explanation: The speaker addresses Justice, an abstraction that cannot hear. Direct address to the absent, the dead or an idea is apostrophe. Personification may sit underneath it — Justice is treated as visitable — but the figure the line is built on is the address itself.

distractorRationale.a: A possible supporting device, but the commanding feature is the vocative O Justice
distractorRationale.c: Nothing is said to *be* something else
distractorRationale.d: There is no like or as

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "Abuja has spoken: the fuel price will rise."
questions.explanation: Abuja, the seat of the federal government, stands in for that government. Naming a thing by something closely associated with it is metonymy. Treating the line as mere personification of a talking city misses the political substitution.

distractorRationale.a: No comparison with like or as
distractorRationale.b: The city is not acting as a character for its own sake; it names an institution
distractorRationale.d: Abuja is talked about, not spoken to

questions.stem: What is the effect of the simile in "The queue at the park gate stretched like a tired snake"?

options.text: It merely decorates the sentence without changing the picture
It makes the length and weariness of the queue visible and slightly threatening
It proves that snakes were present at the park gate
It addresses the queue as if it could hear

questions.explanation: A simile earns its keep by the picture it creates. A tired snake is long, slow and a little dangerous, so the reader feels both the wait and the mood of the crowd. 'To beautify the sentence' is the answer examiners reject.

distractorRationale.a: Effect is never mere decoration in these papers
distractorRationale.c: The comparison is figurative, not a wildlife report
distractorRationale.d: That would be apostrophe; the queue is described, not addressed

questions.stem:
Which statement about the two lines is accurate?
X: "Her voice was silk."
Y: "Her voice was as silk as the evening."

options.text: X is a simile and Y is a metaphor
X is a metaphor and Y is a simile; both compare voice and silk, but only Y announces the comparison
Both are apostrophe because a voice is addressed
Neither is a figure of speech, because silk is a real fabric

questions.explanation: X identifies voice with silk — metaphor. Y uses *as* — simile. The picture is similar; the grammatical test differs. A real fabric can still be used figuratively, and nobody is being addressed in either line.

distractorRationale.a: Reverses the two labels
distractorRationale.c: Apostrophe requires direct address to the absent or abstract
distractorRationale.d: Everyday objects are the usual material of metaphor and simile

questions.stem: In the line "The bar has decided to strike," bar is best explained as

options.text: a simile comparing lawyers to a metal bar
metonymy, using the legal profession's traditional name for the lawyers themselves
apostrophe, because the bar is being spoken to
a literal report that a piece of iron has gone on strike

questions.explanation: In legal register, *the bar* means barristers or the legal profession. The associated name stands for the people. That is metonymy, and the effect is compression: one word carries a whole occupational group. The line is not a comparison with *like*, not an address, and not about metal.

distractorRationale.a: No like or as, and the sense is occupational, not metallic
distractorRationale.c: The bar is the subject of the sentence, not a vocative
distractorRationale.d: A literal reading is absurd, which is a clue that a figure is at work

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: 'Time is a thief.'
questions.explanation: This sentence uses a metaphor to compare time to a thief, suggesting that it steals moments from our lives. Unlike similes, metaphors do not use 'like' or 'as' for comparison.

distractorRationale.a: A simile would require 'like' or 'as' for comparison.
distractorRationale.c: Personification attributes human qualities to non-human entities, which is not the case here.
distractorRationale.d: Apostrophe directly addresses someone who is absent or an abstract idea, which does not apply here.
